Let $z$ represent a token embedding and $\mathbf{z}_t$ its latent representation at time $t$ , with $\mathbf{z}_0 = \mathbf{z}$ and $\mathbf{z}_1 \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I})$ . The joint distribution of the forward process is then given by:

$$
\begin{array}{l} q \left(\boldsymbol {z} _ {> 0}, \tau_ {> 0} \mid \boldsymbol {z} _ {0}\right) := \prod_ {t > 0} q \left(\boldsymbol {z} _ {t}, \tau_ {t} \mid \boldsymbol {z} _ {0}\right) (8) \\ = \prod_ {t > 0} q \left(\boldsymbol {z} _ {t} \mid \boldsymbol {z} _ {0}, \tau_ {t}\right) q \left(\tau_ {t}\right), (9) \\ \end{array}
$$

where

$$
q \left(\boldsymbol {z} _ {t} \mid \boldsymbol {z} _ {0}, \tau_ {t}\right) := \mathcal {N} \left(\boldsymbol {z} _ {t}; \sqrt {\bar {\alpha} (\tau_ {t})} \boldsymbol {z} _ {0}, \bar {\beta} (\tau_ {t}) \mathbf {I}\right),
$$

and $\bar{\alpha} (\cdot)$ and $\bar{\beta} (\cdot)$ denote noise schedules with their domains scaled to [0, 1].

Given $t' = t - \Delta t$ , the reverse process is defined as

$$
\begin{array}{l} p _ {\theta} \left(\boldsymbol {z} _ {0: 1}, \tau_ {0: 1}\right) := p _ {\theta} \left(\boldsymbol {z} _ {1}, \tau_ {1}\right) \prod_ {t ^ {\prime} <   1} p _ {\theta} \left(\boldsymbol {z} _ {t ^ {\prime}}, \tau_ {t ^ {\prime}} \mid \boldsymbol {z} _ {t}, \tau_ {t}\right) (10) \\ = p _ {\theta} \left(\boldsymbol {z} _ {1}, \tau_ {1}\right) \prod_ {t ^ {\prime} <   1} p _ {\theta} \left(\boldsymbol {z} _ {t ^ {\prime}} \mid \boldsymbol {z} _ {t}, \tau_ {t}, \tau_ {t ^ {\prime}}\right) p _ {\theta} \left(\tau_ {t ^ {\prime}} \mid \boldsymbol {z} _ {t}, \tau_ {t}\right). (11) \\ \end{array}
$$

We further parameterize the distribution of $z_{t'}$ as

$$
p _ {\theta} \left(\boldsymbol {z} _ {t ^ {\prime}} \mid \boldsymbol {z} _ {t}, \tau_ {t}, \tau_ {t ^ {\prime}}\right) = q \left(\boldsymbol {z} _ {t ^ {\prime}} \mid \hat {\boldsymbol {z}} _ {0} \left(\boldsymbol {z} _ {t}, \tau_ {t}, t\right), \tau_ {t ^ {\prime}}\right),
$$

where $\hat{z}_0$ is the model prediction of $z_0$ .

Following Ho et al. (2020), the training objective is derived from the variational lower-bound

$$
\begin{array}{l} \mathcal {L} _ {\mathrm {V L B}} = \mathbb {E} _ {q} \left[ - \log \frac {p _ {\theta} \left(\boldsymbol {z} _ {0 : 1} , \tau_ {0 : 1}\right)}{q \left(\boldsymbol {z} _ {> 0} , \tau_ {> 0} \mid \boldsymbol {z} _ {0}\right)} \right] (12) \\ = \mathbb {E} _ {q} \left[ - \log \frac {p _ {\theta} \left(\boldsymbol {z} _ {1} , \tau_ {1}\right)}{q \left(\boldsymbol {z} _ {1} , \tau_ {1} \mid \boldsymbol {z} _ {0}\right)} \right. (13) \\ + \sum_ {0 <   t ^ {\prime} <   1} - \log \frac {q \left(\boldsymbol {z} _ {t ^ {\prime}} \mid \hat {\boldsymbol {z}} _ {0} \left(\boldsymbol {z} _ {t} , \tau_ {t} , t\right) , \tau_ {t ^ {\prime}}\right)}{q \left(\boldsymbol {z} _ {t ^ {\prime}} \mid \boldsymbol {z} _ {0} , \tau_ {t ^ {\prime}}\right)} (14) \\ + \sum_ {0 <   t ^ {\prime} <   1} - \log \frac {p _ {\theta} \left(\tau_ {t ^ {\prime}} \mid \boldsymbol {z} _ {t} , \tau_ {t}\right)}{q \left(\tau_ {t ^ {\prime}}\right)} (15) \\ \left. - \log p _ {\theta} \left(\boldsymbol {z} _ {0}, \tau_ {0} \mid \boldsymbol {z} _ {\Delta t}, \tau_ {\Delta t}\right) \right] (16) \\ = \mathbb {E} _ {q} \left[ \underbrace {\mathbb {K L} \left(q \left(z _ {1} , \tau_ {1} \mid z _ {0}\right) \| p _ {\theta} \left(z _ {1} , \tau_ {1}\right)\right)} _ {\mathcal {L} _ {1}} \right. (17) \\ + \sum_ {0 <   t ^ {\prime} <   1} \underbrace {\mathbb {K L} \left(q \left(\boldsymbol {z} _ {t ^ {\prime}} \mid \boldsymbol {z} _ {0} , \tau_ {t ^ {\prime}}\right) \| q \left(\boldsymbol {z} _ {t ^ {\prime}} \mid \hat {\boldsymbol {z}} _ {0} , \tau_ {t ^ {\prime}}\right)\right)} _ {\mathcal {L} _ {z}} (18) \\ + \sum_ {0 <   t ^ {\prime} <   1} \underbrace {\mathbb {K L} \left(q \left(\tau_ {t ^ {\prime}}\right) \| p _ {\theta} \left(\tau_ {t ^ {\prime}} \mid z _ {t} , \tau_ {t}\right)\right)} _ {\mathcal {L} _ {\tau}} (19) \\ \underbrace {- \log p _ {\theta} \left(\boldsymbol {z} _ {0} , \tau_ {0} \mid \boldsymbol {z} _ {\Delta t} , \tau_ {\Delta t}\right)} _ {\mathcal {L} _ {0}} \Biggr ]. (20) \\ \end{array}
$$

Note that $\mathcal{L}_1$ is a constant and can be ignored, and $\mathcal{L}_0$ also becomes negligible when $\Delta t\to 0$ . According to prior works (Ho et al., 2020; Li et al., 2022), the term $\mathcal{L}_z$ can be simplified as

$$
\mathcal {L} _ {z} = \left\| \hat {\boldsymbol {z}} _ {0} \left(\boldsymbol {z} _ {t}, \tau_ {t}, t\right) - \boldsymbol {z} _ {0} \right\| ^ {2}.
$$

We also add an anchor loss (Gao et al., 2024) $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{anchor}} = \mathbb{E}_q[-\log p_\theta(y|\hat{\boldsymbol{z}}_0(\boldsymbol{z}_t,\tau_t,t))]$ as a regularization term to avoid collapse of the embedding space. Finally, the training objective of the proposed NeoDiff can be written as

$$
\mathcal {L} = \mathcal {L} _ {z} + \mathcal {L} _ {\tau} + \mathcal {L} _ {\text {a n c h o r}}.
$$

We trained our models using NVIDIA RTX 3090 24G GPUs on Ubuntu 18.04 with FairSeq 0.12(Ott et al., 2019)(MIT-licensed). For the WMT14 EnDe and WMT16 En-Ro datasets, training took nearly 4 days and 2 days, respectively, using 4 GPUs. For the IWSLT14 De-En dataset, training took approximately 1 day using a single GPU. The QQP, Wiki-Auto, and QT datasets each required around 8 hours of training on a single GPU. The training data splits are presented in Table 16.

During generation, we used 20 iteration steps $(K = 20)$ without early stopping for the IWSLT14 De-En dataset. For the other datasets, we employed 10 iteration steps without early stopping, which is faster than the 20 steps $(k = 20)$ used by Gao et al. (2024) across all datasets. We utilized 2D parallel decoding and selected the best sentence using the minimum Bayes risk (MBR) (Kumar and Byrne, 2004) method based on the BLEU score. The reported results are averaged over 3 runs. The random seed is set to 7.

We demonstrate NeoDiff's capability for token-level controlled generation while preserving semantic consistency across translations. Given a source sentence $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{src}}$ and its latent representation $\mathbf{z}_0$ , we replace a single token to obtain a modified source $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{src}}'$ . For translation, we initialize the process with $\mathbf{z}_0$ and set $\tau = 1$ only for the modified token position, maximizing noise specifically at that location. This targeted noise application enables precise semantic modifications in the output translation $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{tgt}}'$ while preserving the remaining content. As shown in Table 10, NeoDiff achieves localized modifications, whereas baseline methods like Differmert tend to alter substantial portions of the output sentence. This controlled generation capability stems from our fine-grained noise paradigm, enabling token-specific manipulation of the generation process. review_flags.evidence:
We demonstrate NeoDiff's capability for token-level controlled generation while preserving semantic consistency across translations. Given a source sentence $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{src}}$ and its latent representation $\mathbf{z}_0$ , we replace a single token to obtain a modified source $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{src}}'$ . For translation, we initialize the process with $\mathbf{z}_0$ and set $\tau = 1$ only for the modified token position, maximizing noise specifically at that location.
